book.title: The account in one page
book.text:
Labrynth is a small RegTech company, about 18 people and about $3M in annual revenue, that helps governments and the firms that deal with them get through regulation: it checks permit and licensing applications, builds narrow regulatory assistants and publishes a city-level index of regulatory burden. It is also Supernal's sister company. Both are owned by Infinity Constellation, and the order form names Infinity on both sides of the deal.

Supernal is building Labrynth an Account Management OS: in practice an AI account manager called Cabana Boy that lives in Labrynth's Slack and works for one person, Chris Kuss, the Head of Customer Success. The contract, signed on 29 Jul 2026, is $15,000 a month for 12 months, $180,000 in all, with an exit after month 6. An earlier one-month engagement sits in Account OS as $30,000.

Three things set the account apart. The money is internal to Infinity, so the squad counts it as break-even while it still makes up about 40% of the squad's managed revenue. The scope changed twice before signing, from a content factory to Stuart's priorities to customer success. And progress has been gated less by building than by data access and security, because Labrynth handles sensitive government and nuclear work.

Today the security work is done, the connector is live, and the first workflow, which turns a signed SOW into a kickoff deck, plan and task list, works in testing. The core workflow is due in the first week of December. But Labrynth laid off much of its staff in early November, including its executive team, and has since been folded back into Infinity. The account is at risk.

book.title: Why they bought, and why the scope moved twice
book.text:
The deal began as a handshake between two chief executives inside Infinity: about $100,000 a year, agreed before anyone knew what would be built. Stuart Lacey, Labrynth's CEO, delegated discovery to Harold, his head of product, who steered Supernal toward marketing. By late June the team had a content factory scoped: a knowledge vault, an app and an agent system to produce LinkedIn, X and Substack posts, priced at $7,000 a month.

It did not survive Stuart. When the team finally met him directly on 21 Jul, he said marketing was not his problem. His constraint was delivery capacity: his product and engineering people were saturated, hiring was frozen unless each hire paid for itself, and a new product launch was about to take everyone. He would buy a content factory ready-made, but not wait seven months for one. He asked instead for two things: agents that extend his forward-deployed product and engineering work, and automation of the regulatory index.

What was signed eight days later was neither. It was a system for customer success. The reasons are only partly recorded. Chris had the clearest pain of anyone: about ten parallel projects, no time to keep clients informed or to stop scope creep, and his tools already connected. The account scope fitted Stuart's rule of growing without hiring, since the target was to let Chris take on 12 to 15 accounts instead of 8. One internal note says the client chose this scope. Another says the strategist thought the business case weak. Both are true, and that tension shaped August.
sources: GTM + Scoping, 30 Jun, 2 Jul and 10 Jul 2026

book.title: How the deal is built
book.text:
The signed order form, OF-002, is a monthly fee for strategy and build, $15,000 a month, $180,000 over the term. It describes four monthly milestones: a data foundation and prototype in month 1, an operational pilot with automated client updates in month 2, extension across a cohort of Labrynth's customers in month 3, and a portfolio command center with a calibrated expectation scorecard in month 4. After that, the fee continues for maintenance and refinement. There are no numeric success targets other than an expectation score of 3 or better.

The parties line is unusual: Infinity Constellation trading as Supernal, selling to Infinity Constellation trading as Labrynth, billed to Infinity's finance team. That is why the squad calls it break-even and internal, and why Account OS showed no revenue for it. Stuart had said he was open to cash, trade or equity, and that the money was not his worry.

The order form puts a lot on the client. Sameen Kashfi approves, Chris runs day to day, and Labrynth must supply a pilot account, the contract repository, ClickUp, Granola and Notion within five business days of a request, keep task statuses accurate, and attend a weekly working session. Delays move dates day for day. Labrynth owns the strategy, code and workflows; Supernal runs the infrastructure.

Delivery has not followed the month-by-month plan. The client deck re-cut the work into strategy, a pilot, a security phase and a workflow build, because security was not in the order form but became the gate for everything.

book.title: The product and why it is built this way
book.text:
The first prototype in August was a conventional app. By early September it had become something else: a Hermes agent connected to Slack, where Chris already works, with the app kept only as a panel to configure and watch the agent. Hermes was chosen because memory, skills and connections came ready-made, and Chris liked it more than the app. The squad chose to invest in the agent's skills and in Chris's way of writing before tuning the knowledge store, so that the agent could improve over time and Chris could one day own it.

Security drove the next two months. Labrynth works with government and nuclear clients and was cautious about letting an outside system read its meetings and contracts. An early incident, an agent messaging Chris unprompted in a shared channel, did not help. The team chose restricted access over redaction, then designed a Smart Connector: a gateway that holds the credentials, logs every action and keeps each Labrynth client switched off until Labrynth turns it on. Twelve security items were closed between 15 and 30 Oct, and the connector went live on ClickUp and Granola on 30 Oct.

The work now centres on one core workflow. The Kickoff Kit reads a signed SOW and drafts a kickoff deck, an 8-week plan and a ClickUp list, asking questions instead of guessing; a checker refuses any date, name or owner without a source. The Daily Delivery Check will then review each account every day. This pair was put first because it carries most of the modeled value, and because Chris needs to see it beat simply prompting the agent.
sources: Weekly Review + Next Cycle Plan, 11 Sep and 23 Oct 2026

book.title: How delivery has gone
book.text:
The first week was the low point. The weekly report rated the account critical: Chris said plainly he was not sure this was the right thing to build, access to contracts, ClickUp and transcripts was pending, and privacy concerns were open. Within a week Chris was suggesting a pivot, and the issue went to Ryan, Scott and Tauseef. The strategist wanted to leave the account.

Two things turned it. Process maps of how Chris works today and could work tomorrow landed well on 17 Aug, and a business case built with Chris was approved by him and Sameen by 24 Aug. Vitor, the lead engineer, then moved quickly: agent deployed by 11 Sep, Chris onboarded on Slack around 22 Sep.

From late September to late October the work was held by security. Only one client's data was in the system, wider access needed approval, and the squad itself flagged 19 and then 23 open security alerts in the repository. The team estimated that approval would unlock about four weeks of work. Chris approved the approach on 15 Oct, the controls were tested by 22 Oct, and the connector went live on 30 Oct. Chris was pleased with the pace.

Since then the build has moved and the inputs have not. Chris has not shared real SOWs, Granola access is limited to two public folders, and the 5 Nov session moved to 10 Nov. The team used a synthetic SOW to keep going. Measured against the order form, which expected portfolio scale by month 3, delivery is about two months behind, with the core workflow due in early December.
sources: Delivery Sync, 17 Aug, 24 Aug and 21 Sep 2026
Squad Lab, 22 Sep, 13 Oct and 20 Oct 2026

book.title: The people
book.text:
At the start, Labrynth's people pulled in different directions. Stuart Lacey, the CEO, was the sponsor who had made the deal but had not spoken to anyone at Supernal until 21 Jul; when he did, he set priorities himself and blamed the earlier misdirection on his delegate. Harold, head of product and a former colleague from another company, had routed Supernal to marketing; he has not been engaged since August. Daniel Zaitsev, head of marketing, owned the content need that was dropped. Renan Lima, head of engineering, says little but must approve anything that touches Labrynth's systems, and he holds the Granola access Chris needs. Athena reviewed security. Sameen Kashfi signed off as executive sponsor on the order form.

Chris Kuss is the account. He is the only user, the source of every requirement and the person who must share SOWs and access. He started doubtful, became engaged once the maps and business case reflected his work, and keeps testing whether Cabana Boy does more than a general assistant would. He prefers workflows to metrics and has a deep backlog of his own clients to serve.

The November layoffs changed the map. Labrynth's executive team is gone and Stuart is out. Chris remains the contact, but who now sponsors the work and pays for it is unknown. Seb heard on 13 Nov that Labrynth has been folded back into Infinity.

On Supernal's side, Ryan holds the commercial relationship and Scott the original handshake. Jaime leads strategy and owns the weekly brief. Vitor leads the build, with Harvy and Peter added in November. Diana is the other strategist in the squad. Katie, Devan and Thomas know Chris personally and were named as backup levers.

book.title: What the account means for the squad
book.text:
Labrynth is one of four accounts run by Supernal's first squad, The Origin: Jaime and Diana as strategists, Vitor and Harvy as engineers, carrying Ethic Select, Hooray, Super73 and Labrynth together. The squad is measured on leverage, managed revenue divided by its cost. Labrynth's $180,000 is the largest single line, about 40% of the squad's roughly $455,000, and it holds the squad's leverage at 1.20x. Without it, leverage falls to 0.73x, well below the 1.5x goal.

That makes the account matter more than its internal, break-even revenue suggests. It is also where the squad learned things it now reuses. The Hermes agent pattern was meant to be recycled for other clients. The way the team handled Chris's first 90 days, a clear pace and a measurable result, became the model for onboarding a new college client. The security checklist and connector design answer questions other clients will ask.

The risk runs the other way too. Vitor's time has been split between Labrynth and Super73, and the squad added Harvy to Labrynth in November partly to cover that. If Labrynth's fees stop or shrink after the layoffs, the squad's numbers change sharply.

book.title: What value has shown, and what is next
book.text:
There is no measured value yet. The business case, shared with Chris on 23 Oct, models $605,000 to $839,000 a year across the planned workflows. The core workflow alone is modeled at $376,000 to $444,000: 1,364 to 2,069 hours returned, worth $76,000 to $144,000, plus $300,000 of renewal protection that the team itself marks as needing validation. Four inputs to that case are still unconfirmed by Chris. The one measured number is speed: under four minutes from a SOW to a kickoff deck, on a synthetic SOW.

Chris's baseline is clear: he runs about 8 engagements and spends 80 to 90% of his time on QA and demo preparation, against a normal 10 to 25%. Nobody has yet measured whether Cabana Boy changes that. Usage is one person who logs in when prompted.

What happens next depends less on the build than on Labrynth's situation. The 10 Nov session with Chris was meant to show the full flow and to confirm whether the account continues after the layoffs; its outcome is not recorded in any source read. If the work continues, the next steps are real SOWs, full Granola access, ClickUp write access with its own security review, and the core workflow in the first week of December. Commercially, the strategist was to alert Ryan before the session and bring in Devan if revenue was affected. With Labrynth folded back into Infinity, the decision may sit with Infinity, not Labrynth. The month-6 exit window opens about early February 2027.

answers.q: Is anyone still paying for this?
answers.a: Unknown. The contract is $15,000 a month between two Infinity companies and the squad counts it as break-even. After the early-Nov layoffs took out Labrynth's executive team and Labrynth was folded back into Infinity, the 10 Nov session was meant to confirm continuity; its outcome is not recorded.

Inputs and security, not the build. Most of Sep and Oct went to security approval and the Smart Connector, closed on 30 Oct. Since then Chris has not shared real SOWs and Granola access is limited to two folders, so the team builds on a synthetic SOW.

answers.q: What does Chris need to see?
answers.a: That the workflow beats prompting the agent himself, and why it is better than Claude. The core workflow turns a SOW into a kickoff deck, plan and task list in under 4 minutes and is due in the first week of Dec; he also needs a verified SOC 2 answer.
